title: The Year Covoiturage.fr Asked Its Passengers to Pay
dek: After five years of business models that did not pay, the French carpooling site began charging travellers to book online, and some members called for a boycott.

story.founder: Frédéric Mazzella, Francis Nappez, Nicolas Brusson
story.event: Abandoning a free service funded by company platforms and advertising for paid online booking with a commission
story.summary: Covoiturage.fr, run by Frédéric Mazzella's company Comuto, was free for travellers and lived on advertising and white-label platforms sold to companies, which by Mazzella's account were little used and kept falling in price. After what he counts as six business models between 2006 and 2011, the company began testing paid online booking with a commission in 2011; some users called for a boycott, but the company said no-shows fell from 35 per cent of bookings to below 4 per cent by June 2012, and the service, renamed BlaBlaCar, kept growing.
paragraphs: In 2009, three years after buying the carpooling site covoiturage.fr and relaunching it, Frédéric Mazzella paid himself a salary for the first time. His company, Comuto, took in about €140,000 that year and lost about €110,000, according to its published accounts as summarised in a 2016 business-school case. He had two partners by then: Francis Nappez, who ran the technology, and Nicolas Brusson, whom he had met at the INSEAD business school.

For travellers the site was free. Drivers posted journeys, passengers contacted them, and the two settled costs between themselves. The money came from elsewhere: some advertising, and white-label versions of the platform sold to companies such as Ikea, MAIF and Vinci Park for their staff or customers. Mazzella later said about 200 companies took one, but they were little used, and firms would not pay for quality, so prices kept falling. The long-distance trips that made up almost all the site's traffic earned nothing; revenue, he said, grew in a straight line while costs grew exponentially. By his count the company tried six business models between 2006 and 2011.

The change they settled on was to charge the travellers themselves. Passengers would book and pay for a seat online in advance, and the site would keep a percentage; anyone cancelling less than a day before lost the fare, half of which went to the driver. The case study reports that Pierre Kosciusko-Morizet, founder of the marketplace PriceMinister and a co-founder of ISAI, a fund that invested €1.25 million in Comuto in 2010, suggested it. Testing began in 2011. Some longtime users felt betrayed, and a Facebook group called for a boycott. Mazzella's answer, as France's intellectual property office later recorded it, was that many people believe everything online is free, but a business model had to be found.

The company said no-shows had hit 35 per cent of bookings before the change. By June 2012, when the booking system was extended across France ahead of the summer holidays, it put them below 4 per cent, and Mazzella said the reliability gave carpooling new momentum. The site had passed a million members in April 2011. Renamed BlaBlaCar, it claimed 20 million members in 19 countries by late 2015, the year it raised $200 million.

quote.text: Every thinking bushi knew well enough that money formed the sinews of war; but he did not think of raising the appreciation of money to a virtue.
quote.locator: Chapter X, "Education and Training of a Samurai"
quote.source_title: Bushido, the Soul of Japan, Project Gutenberg eBook #12096
quote.connection: Nitobe's samurai accepted that money was necessary while refusing to admire it. Covoiturage.fr's members had shared costs with no one taking a cut, and Mazzella decided a cut was what would keep the service alive. Nitobe's distinction does not say who was right; it only separates needing money from honouring it.

reflection: Charging for something people once had free can feel like a betrayal, and some of covoiturage.fr's members said so plainly. What answered them in the end was not an argument but a service that worked better: a seat that was still there when the passenger arrived.

Nitobe would remind you that needing money and admiring it are different things. You can ask a fair price for work done well without letting the price become the point. If there is something you keep giving away because asking feels awkward, it may help to notice whether the awkwardness is about the money or about a quiet doubt that the work is worth it.
invitation: Choose one thing you give away, at work or at home, that costs you more than you usually admit. Write down what a fair exchange for it would be, even if you decide not to ask for it yet.

sources.title: BlaBlaCar, les secrets de la licorne (case study by G. Dang Nguyen for the MOOC Economie collaborative, 2016)
sources.supports: Mazzella bought covoiturage.fr in 2006 and launched his version in July 2006; Brusson met at INSEAD; Comuto revenue of about €140,000 and a net loss of about €110,000 in 2009 from published accounts; free service for the public, revenue from advertising (about 10 per cent) and white-label partnerships with Ikea, MAIF, Vinci Park and others; Mazzella's remark (to Wired) that companies would not pay for quality and prices had to fall; Kosciusko-Morizet reportedly suggesting a model in which the public paid; ISAI set up by business angels including Kosciusko-Morizet; booking paid in advance, refund only if cancelled at least 24 hours ahead, otherwise half to the driver; payment tested from early 2011; users feeling betrayed and a Facebook boycott group; no-shows of 35 per cent before; more than a million members by 2011

research_notes: Number of business models: Mazzella told Journal du Net (2021) six between 2006 and 2011, Maddyness (2020) says six, and the 2016 case study says he told Atlantico 'six or seven'; the story uses his own count of six. Timing of paid booking: INPI and the case study put the turning point in 2011 (the case says it was tested in Brittany at the start of 2011 and extended across France in the second half of 2011); Journal de l'Automobile (19 June 2012) says testing began in May 2011 and the national rollout came in June 2012; Wikipedia and the French Tech Journal date the service to 2012. The story says testing began in 2011 and that booking was extended across France by June 2012, following the contemporary trade report. No-shows: all sources agree on 35 per cent before; the case study says under 3 per cent after, Journal de l'Automobile (company figures, June 2012) under 4 per cent, INPI 'divided by ten'; the story uses the conservative 'below 4 per cent' and attributes it to the company. Commission level: the case study says it started at 7 per cent and rose to about 10 and then 12 per cent; INPI says about 11 per cent; the story gives no rate. ISAI amount: ITespresso (June 2010) and TechCrunch give €1.25 million, the case study €1.5 million; the story uses the contemporary €1.25 million. Revenue: the case study gives €140,000 revenue and a €110,000 net loss for 2009 from published accounts; Journal du Net reports Mazzella saying the company platforms brought about €1 million in revenue between 2008 and 2010, which would imply a much larger 2010; the story uses only the 2009 figures and leaves out the €1 million. The suggestion by Pierre Kosciusko-Morizet rests on the case study, which puts it in the conditional, so the story attributes it to the case. Rename: Maddyness dates the rename to 2011 and INPI implies 2013; the BlaBlaCar name was first used for the UK launch in June 2011 (TechCrunch), so the story does not date the French rename. Membership: TechCrunch says 1 million users in April 2011, the case study 1.3 million by the end of 2011, INPI about a million when the commission arrived. Mazzella's remarks are in French and are given in English paraphrase rather than as direct quotations. Wired, L'Express and Rue89 articles cited by the case study could not be read here and are not cited. The case-study PDF was read through a local text extraction because the page renderer could not open it. The Nitobe line comes from his discussion of the samurai's disdain for money in the chapter on education and training.
